decisions.why: Jerusalem is a single addressee, not God: tu (rule 3), as the Latin's singular 'Lauda'. The Latin has no 'O'. The build is 112:1's ('Louvai, meninos, o Senhor', no 'ó'), so the same here. Row 'vocative plural of persons' (28:1) supplies 'ó' where a vocative can be heard as the object; here 'o Senhor' follows at once and the comma is sung, so it is left out, keeping the two colons alike as in the Latin. The Brazilian lectionary/LH line is 'Glorifica o Senhor, Jerusalém … celebra teu Deus, ó Sião' (circulation.md): from the Hebrew's verb; the Latin's is laudáre → louvar. Neighbour, seen at the finish: Ps 145:10 took the stylist's 'o teu Deus, ó Sião' (so that Sião is not heard as in apposition to God). No reader of 147:1 raised it; 'Sião' is left bare here as the Latin, and whoever wants the two alike adds 'ó' in the second colon — a particle, not re-read by a gate.

decisions.latin: Qui pósuit … Qui emíttit … Qui dat … Qui annúntiat
decisions.why: Four relative clauses hang from the God of 147:1 with no main verb (147:6–7 then go on with plain verbs, 'Mittit … Emíttet'). A bare 'Que pôs … Que envia … Que dá' at the head of a verse is heard as a question ('Que dá?') or a wish; MS1932 makes each a cleft ('É ele que'). The draft names the subject in a main clause, 'Ele …', four times, as 65:9 ('Ele pôs a minha alma para a vida') and 134:10 ('Ele feriu') did: the Latin's anaphora is kept as a repeated 'Ele', the relative is grammar (D2). Neighbours, seen at the finish: Ps 145:7a has 'Ele guarda' (the same choice, against a Latinist minor asking 'Que guarda'); Ps 146 (drafted in parallel) keeps the bare relative 'Que cura … Que conta … Que dá'. 146:9 'Qui dat' and 147:5 'Qui dat' therefore differ: for the main session to align (one touch here: option 3).

decisions.why: Sera is the bar put across a door (L&S). 106:16 'vectes férreos' is 'as trancas de ferro', and the glossary row (vectis) notes that 147:2 is another word. The Greek has μοχλούς in both places, so D15's test would allow one word; but the Latin has two and 'ferrolhos' costs nothing: it is plain, MS1932's, and one blind reader did not know 'trancas' (106:16). v1 ambiguity reader listed 'ferrolhos' as unknown; 'trancas' was unknown to another (106:16). Both are the concrete word; no plainer name for a door-bar exists. Held.

decisions.why: A double accusative: 'set your borders (as) peace' (Greek ὁ τιθεὶς τὰ ὅριά σου εἰρήνην, the same build). 43:14 'Posuísti nos oppróbrium' became 'Fizestes de nós uma afronta', but 'fez das tuas fronteiras a paz' is not a sentence anyone says. The draft moves the peace into the object and the borders into a place, as both Vulgate-family versions do (DRB 'hath placed peace in thy borders', MS1932 'estabeleceu a paz nas tuas fronteiras'): words and image kept, grammar changed (D2). This is the line of the Corpus Christi and Marian Vespers; the Brazilian LH/lectionary has 'A paz em teus limites garantiu' (circulation.md, Hebrew-based). 'fines' of a city's territory is 'fronteiras'; the glossary's 'confins' (7:7a, 'fines terræ' → 'os confins da terra') is heard in Brazil as the far ends of the earth, and 'os teus confins' as remote corners. v2 Latinist gate (minor): the frontier become peace is slightly flattened; he asks 'Ele fez das tuas fronteiras a paz' — option 2, held for the reason above.

decisions.why: The same noun phrase as 80:17 'ex ádipe fruménti' → 'da gordura do trigo', so the same words (rule 6); the adeps row keeps the concrete fat (rule 5), and saturáre/satiáre → saciar. The Brazilian LH and lectionary say 'a flor do trigo' (circulation.md) — the Hebrew idiom's sense 'the finest', and MS1932's 'da flor da farinha'; kept as an option because it is the line Brazilians know from Corpus Christi, but it replaces the Latin's image with its meaning. v2: the stylist found the fronted object with the clitic at the end ('e da gordura do trigo te sacia') translated-sounding and asked for the natural order, which ends the colon on the image; taken (order, D2). The ambiguity reader heard 'gordura do trigo' as puzzling, literal fat — the Latin's image, kept (rule 5); 'flor do trigo' stays the option.

decisions.latin: Qui emíttit elóquium suum terræ: * velóciter currit sermo ejus
decisions.why: One of the verses D15 and D26 left to decide locally: elóquium (λόγιον) and sermo (λόγος) side by side, and three verses on, verbum (λόγος again) twice → 'palavra'. D15's test keeps apart what the Greek keeps apart: sermo and verbum are one word (palavra), elóquium is another. Outside Ps 118 elóquium has gone to 'palavra' where it stood alone (11:7, 17:31, 104:19, 106:11); here that would give 'a sua palavra … a sua palavra' in one verse where the Latin varies. The draft uses D26's clause in the present, as 103:34 'o que digo': 'Ele envia à terra o que diz' — an object, so no genitive forces a noun. MS1932 'as suas ordens' interprets. v2: both the Latinist (minor: a noun object turned into a clause) and the stylist (worst line: a thin gloss, flat at the mediant) asked, each on his own, for 'a sua fala'. Taken: it keeps D15's distinction (λόγιον apart from λόγος, which is 'palavra' here and in 147:7–8) with a noun. Cost: in 55:11 'fala' rendered sermo (beside verbum); here it renders elóquium beside sermo — 'fala' is the psalter's second word for speech where two stand together, not a fixed equivalent. Proposed as such in the glossary.

options.label: a sua fala
options.note: v2 — the Latinist's and the stylist's fix, independently: a noun, kept apart from sermo → palavra in the next colon

options.label: o que diz
options.note: v1 — D26's clause, present as 103:34; the stylist's worst line, the Latinist's minor

options.label: a sua palavra
options.note: as 11:7, 104:19 where elóquium stood alone; here it would repeat 'palavra' in the verse where the Latin varies

options.note: the noun D16 tried; refused by the stylist nine times in Pss 11 and 118

decisions.why: v1 copied 129:3's 'quem subsistirá?' (same two Latin words). Here the verb has a thing to bear — the cold before which one stands — and the sustinére row (D36) gives 'suportar' where the object is a thing to endure (68:8; the row also names 129:3). The Latinist (minor) asked 'quem o suportará?', the stylist 'quem resistirá?' ('subsistirá' bookish), and the ambiguity reader did not know 'subsistirá'. Taken: 'quem suportará?', the row's verb, absolute as the Latin (the object is left implied, as 'sustinébit' leaves it). 'resistirá' (MS1932) is refused as a word of opposition, not of bearing; kept as an option. Consequence: 129:3 now differs from this line; whoever rules the row should say whether 129:3 follows (proposed in the glossary).

decisions.why: Spíritus (πνεῦμα) is wind and spirit at once; in the thaw it is the wind first, and DRB and MS1932 both say 'wind'. The row of 102:16 chose 'sopro' to keep both, but here the verb is 'flabit' and 'soprará o seu sopro' makes a figure the Latin does not have (the Greek does: πνεύσει τὸ πνεῦμα). The draft keeps the Latin's word, 'espírito', lower case as D44 (50:13) and 142:10b: the Latin leaves the Spirit audible and 'vento' would close it. The ambiguity reader should say whether the wind is still heard. v1 ambiguity reader: both readings listed, 'his Spirit, in a spiritual sense' likely heard first — so the ambiguity is kept, leaning the other way from the context. Held: 'vento' would close what the Latin leaves open; it stays option 1.

decisions.why: 'Non … omni' is literally 'not to every nation', a Hebraism for 'to none (other)'. The draft keeps the Latin's form: 'Não fez assim com toda nação' says what is meant — this was not done for every nation, only for Israel — without supplying 'outra'. v2 takes two v1 remarks together: the Latinist (minor) asked the singular back ('a toda nação'), and the stylist found 'fazer assim a' unidiomatic and asked 'com'. The ambiguity reader heard 'not the same for the other nations', with room left for 'not all, only some' — that room is the Latin's own.

choices.147:1: No title: DO's Psalm147.txt begins at 'Lauda, Jerúsalem'; it has no 'Allelúja' line (the LXX has αλληλουια Αγγαιου καὶ Ζαχαριου; MS1932 prints 'Aleluia'). Nothing to translate under D7. 'Sião' as the glossary.
choices.147:2: Quóniam → Porque (default). confortáre → fortalecer, the verb of the confortári row. The second colon has no 'and', as the Latin.
choices.147:3: saturáre/satiáre → saciar (row). v2: the natural order, verb before its complement (stylist).
choices.147:4: velóciter → depressa (row); the Latin's order kept, adverb first, so the colon ends on 'palavra' (sermo → palavra, D15).
choices.147:5: 'dá' for 'dat', the Latin's plain verb (MS1932 'faz cair' explains). nébula → névoa (ὁμίχλη, mist; the Hebrew's frost not followed).
choices.147:6: Mittit → Lança (βάλλοντος, throwing; as the míttere rows 21:18, 80:15) kept apart from emíttere → enviar (147:4, 147:7; row of 103:10).
choices.147:7: 'Emíttet verbum suum, et liquefáciet ea' is built as 106:20 'Misit verbum suum, et sanávit eos' → 'Enviou a sua palavra, e os curou'; so 'Enviará a sua palavra, e os derreterá'. 'ea' (neuter plural: the snow, mist and ice) → 'os'. liquefácere → derreter (row of 74:4). Soft flag: second colon +4 by the counter, which does not elide; sung, 'seu‿espírito' and 'e‿correrão' close it to about +2. Accepted: nothing can go without losing a word of the Latin. The ambiguity reader found 'os' without a clear antecedent ('gelo' is singular); the Latin's 'ea' is as loose (neuter plural for snow, mist and ice together). Held. The futures are the Latin's.
choices.147:8: Jacob → Jacó; judícia → juízos (D15). Soft flag: first colon +4 by the counter; 'Ele‿anuncia‿a sua' elides to about +2. The named subject 'Ele' (decision qui) costs the rest.
choices.147:9: manifestáre → manifestar (row of 79:2b). The object moved after the verb (natural order, D2); the Latin puts 'judícia sua' first. Soft flag: second colon -3 (the Latin's long 'manifestávit'); accepted. The ambiguity reader heard 'os seus juízos' as God's, rightly. v2 soft flag: first colon -3 ('com toda nação', 9 against the Latin's 12); accepted: nothing is missing, the Latin's words are longer.
